sections.html:
Land records are filed at Records Intake, Room B20 of the historic Tarrant County Courthouse, 100 W. Weatherford St., Fort Worth, TX 76196. Land-related documents can be recorded only there, not at the sub-courthouses.

There are three ways to file: walk in between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday; mail the original with a check or money order payable to the Tarrant County Clerk; or use eRecording. In-person filers show a driver's license or ID. Mailed documents need no copy of one.

Clerks cannot notarize a document, give legal advice or help you fill in a form, so get the deed notarized before you arrive. Intake takes only originals or clerk-certified copies.

Most documents cost $20 for the first page and $4 for each added page. A notice of trustee sale is $10. A sheet printed on both sides counts as two pages.

Tarrant County Clerk fees
ServiceFee
Recording, first page$20
Recording, each added page$4
Notice of trustee sale$10
Copy made in person or by mail, per page$1
Certification of a copy, added$5
Unofficial watermarked copy onlineFree

You can pay with cash, credit card, check or money order. A card adds a small convenience fee. A few document types are exceptions to the standard fee, so ask the clerk or check the fee schedule for yours.

The County Clerk Official Records Search is free to browse. Once you find a document, you can register for an account and download an unofficial watermarked copy at no charge, which is enough for your own research.

A title company or lender may want a certified copy. Pick the certified-copy icon online, pay the calculated fee, then collect the file under Order History in your account. Certified copies are also sold in person at Room B30 of the courthouse, or by mail with a self-addressed stamped envelope and the document number.

New filings take a few days to appear. Recorded documents generally show up on the search site 5 to 7 business days after recording. Intake scans and indexes while you wait and gives you an instrument number, so ask for it if you need to prove the filing sooner. Clerks do not run title searches, lien searches or restriction reviews. A title company does that work.

Intake takes documents that the law authorizes or permits to be recorded, mainly those tied to land. Deeds, deeds of trust, liens and lien releases, certain land-related affidavits and plats are the core examples.

The clerk turns away these categories:

  • Documents with no statutory authority behind their filing.
  • Documents that are not regular on their face.
  • Documents not properly signed in front of an officer such as a notary.
  • Copies that are neither originals nor clerk-certified.

Wills get special treatment. Intake records only probated wills, and anyone who wants a will kept at the courthouse can leave it with the Probate office in Room B90 for a $5 fee. Texas law requires a conveyance to be signed and acknowledged, or sworn before two witnesses, before it can be recorded. The deed types seen most often are general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds.

sections.h2: Why records matter when you sell
sections.html:
A buyer's title company reads the recorded chain on your parcel before closing, and anything unreleased can delay the sale. Watch for an old deed of trust with no release, a recorded lien, an affidavit that clouds title, or a missing deed from an inherited property.

A tax lien needs no recording to exist. The state tax lien attaches on January 1 each year, and a buyer cannot get clear title until delinquent taxes are paid. State tax liens filed by the comptroller are recorded with the county clerk, so those can show in the clerk's records too.

When a lender starts foreclosure, a notice of trustee sale appears in the clerk's records. Texas foreclosure sales are auctions. For a tax foreclosure, a constable or an agent hired by the taxing unit runs the sale. If a recorded notice names your house, you still have routes: pay off the debt, sell through a listing, or take a cash offer that closes before the sale date.

The county clerk acts as county recorder, clerk of the commissioners court, and the office that takes probate filings such as applications and small estate affidavits. In Tarrant County the real property side and the probate side sit in different rooms of the same courthouse, with probate in Room B90.

That split matters when a house came to you through a death. The heirs may need probate papers on file before a deed can be signed, and those papers live in a different queue from the deed. Plan a trip or a mailing for each, and ask the title company which papers it needs recorded before closing.

Title companies and escrow agents have account options too. The county offers an OPR Escrow Payments route, with 817-884-1062 for completing the process after an online payment, and a bulk data payment route at 817-884-1069. Most individual sellers never need either, but your title company might use the first.

Tarrant County has a Property Fraud Alert sign-up on its Real Estate Records page. Use the link there to see how alerts work.

A practical habit is to search your own name and address on the Official Records Search once or twice a year. Look for deeds or liens you do not recognize. If you find one, bring the instrument number to the clerk's office and to a title company.

Recording is public by design. That helps buyers and lenders trust the chain of title, but it also means anyone can see what was filed against your parcel, and a forged deed that gets recorded still has to be unwound through the courts.

sections.h2: Before you list: a records checklist
sections.html:
A few minutes of searching can save a closing. Pull your own deed from the Official Records Search and confirm the names and legal description match what will go on the contract. Look for any deed of trust from a past loan and make sure a release was recorded. Search for liens filed against you.

If anything shows up, bring the instrument number to your title company early. A release can take time to arrive, and a cash buyer can often work around a messy file faster than a lender can, though the title still has to clear before the deed changes hands.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Tarrant County?
faqs.a: Most documents cost $20 for the first page and $4 for each added page. A sheet printed on both sides counts as two pages.

faqs.q: Where is the Tarrant County Clerk's records office?
faqs.a: Records Intake is in Room B20 of the Tarrant County Courthouse, 100 W. Weatherford St., Fort Worth, TX 76196. Hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed by mail in Tarrant County?
faqs.a: Yes. Mail the original to Room B20 with a check or money order payable to the Tarrant County Clerk, and work out the fee from the page count. The deed must already be notarized.

faqs.q: Can I get a copy of my deed for free?
faqs.a: Yes, an unofficial watermarked copy downloads free from the Official Records Search once you register. Certified copies cost $1 per page plus $5 for certification.

faqs.q: How long before a recorded deed shows online in Tarrant County?
faqs.a: Generally 5 to 7 business days after recording. In-person filers get an instrument number and proof of recording while they wait.
